newsitem.title: USA: Consumer prices post modest April gain.
newsitem.headline: Consumer prices post modest April gain.

text.p: Consumer prices advanced modestly in April, the government said on Thursday, offering more proof that inflation remains largely in check.
The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose 0.1 percent last month, matching the 0.1 percent rise in March.
Excluding the volatile food and energy sector, the so-called core rate of inflation advanced 0.3 percent after rising by 0.2 percent in March.
Wall Street had predicted the overall index would rise by 0.1 percent, but economists had expected the core rate to climb by just 0.2 percent.
"The numbers were a tad disappointing," Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said.
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co., agreed, calling the consumer price data "a little bit disappointing."
"In my opinion, it is more than enough justification for the Fed to move next week."
Federal Reserve policymakers, who raised interest rates at their last meeting in March to head off possible inflation, will meet again next week.
The consumer price data follow Wednesday's release of a report showing producer prices falling by 0.6 percent in April.
The Labour Department said the larger gain in the April core rate of consumer prices reflected an upturn in the index for apparel and upkeep.

Apparel costs jumped 0.9 percent last month after falling 0.3 percent in March. The department said the April increase in apparel prices was the biggest since February 1993, when prices rose 1.1 percent.
The department said April energy prices fell 1.5 percent after falling 1.7 percent in March, while food prices dropped by 0.2 percent after being unchanged the month before.
Fresh fruit prices fell 1.0 percent, while fresh vegetables dropped 9.1 percent.
Transportation costs declined by 0.4 percent in April after edging up 0.1 percent the month before. Gasoline prices fell 2.6 percent.
Prices of tobacco and smoking products rose 2.4 percent in April, the biggest increase in nearly seven years. In July 1990 tobacco prices were up 2.5 percent.
Housing prices rose 0.2 percent after being unchanged in March.

In another report, the department said fewer Americans entered unemployment lines for the first time in the week ended May 10. First-time jobless claims fell to 319,000 from 350,000 in the previous week.
The four-week moving average of claims, viewed as a more reliable gauge of employment trends, fell to 333,500 from 336,750.
The total number of people continuing to collect jobless benefits rose by 23,000 to 2,314,000 in the week ended May 3, the latest period for which that data were available.
